abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Dye-decolorizing peroxidases (DyPs) represent a distinct family of heme peroxidases with unique capabilities in dye decolorization, lignin synthesis, and lignin degradation. While traditional phylogenetics and structural alignments have categorized DyPs into four distinct subclasses (A-D), the secret to unlocking their industrial versatility lies in the ability to understand and re-engineer the sophisticated architecture of their active sites. This review critically analyzed findings from 35 peer-reviewed articles (2007–2025) sourced from eight electronic databases, examining 93 distinct mutations within 20 different DyPs. Moving beyond basic classification, this study identifies hotspots that influence DyP performance, examining how site-directed mutagenesis affects structural integrity, H2O2 tolerance, and catalytic potential. Central among these is the histidine-arginine-aspartate (H-R-D) triad, which mediates the formation of high-valent intermediates in a class-specific manner. Analysis reveals that 29% of the studied variants surpassed their wild-type counterparts in catalytic efficiency, with a few variants achieving rare and desirable improvements in stability and an alkaline shift in optimal working pH. Mapping these mutational effects identifies the critical surface-exposed motifs and gatekeeping amino acids that govern long-range electron transfer and substrate accessibility. Since rate-limiting steps are substrate-dependent, a single mutation might produce diverse catalytic outcomes. Beyond clarifying structure–function relationships, these findings aim to provide a strategic blueprint for directed evolution. Identifying these catalytic hotspots guides the precision engineering of DyPs with tailored specificity and enhanced characteristics. Overall, this work acts as a catalyst for future protein engineering, unlocking a new era of robust biocatalysts capable of withstanding the harsh environments of modern industrial biotechnology.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Peroxidases constitute a broad category of oxidoreductases that are found in various prokaryotic and eukaryotic species. They catalyze the oxidation of a wide range of organic substrates and inorganic substances, with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as the electron acceptor. Most of the peroxidases that have been characterized are hemoproteins, which have heme as an essential prosthetic group for their catalytic activity.

Traditionally, heme peroxidases have been classified into two large superfamilies: plant and animal peroxidases. Of these, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) is the model plant peroxidase and has been extensively studied for over a hundred years. Around three decades ago, a distinct superfamily of heme peroxidases, the dye-decolorizing peroxidases (DyPs), was discovered in various fungal and bacterial species. Dye-decolorizing enzymes have been of great interest due to their great oxidative potential, especially toward peroxidase-recalcitrant dyes, stability in acidic conditions, availability in nature, and ease of expression in industrial host organisms. ,

The first DyP protein was extracted from the soil fungus Thanatephorus cucumeris (formerly Geotrichum candidum Dec 1), namely DyP Dec 1. Despite this fact, databases such as InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/) and RedoxiBase (https://peroxibase.toulouse.inra.fr/) reflect a bacterial bias among this family of enzymes (Figure A). Phylogenetic analysis (Figure B), as annotated within RedoxiBase, segregates DyPs into four subclasses: A, B, C, and D, based on sequence similarity. ,−
In fact, the previous classification was only based on the amino acid (AA) sequence, which was not very effective for studying the catalytic mechanism and active sites. In light of these discrepancies, Yoshida and Sugano recommended a new classification scheme based on their overall structure (primary and tertiary structures) using the multiple three-dimensional alignment tool MATRAS for structure-based sequence alignment. This newer classification segregates DyPs into three classes (P “primitive”, I “intermediate” and V “advanced”). , In 2023, Yoshida and Sugano further subdivided each class into four subclasses (1–4) to allow a more detailed understanding of DyPs origin and characteristics.

sec.p: Despite their sequence divergence, all four DyP subtypes (A, B, C, and D) share a conserved tertiary structure with two ferredoxin-like folds and heme buried in their molecules. Sequencing analysis of the four DyP subfamilies revealed various well-conserved residues situated around the heme active site, which are predicted to play significant roles in catalysis. The functional role of these residues, however, is apparently enzyme-class-dependent and varies in the phylogenetic subclasses A, B, C, and D.

DyPs exhibit notable catalytic diversity despite sharing a conserved heme-dependent catalytic core. Their primary activity resembles that of the classical peroxidase cycle. Both integrate a ferric resting state that is oxidized by H2O2 to form two major transient intermediates: compound I and compound II (Figure ), which mediate the oxidation of a broad range of substrates. These include recalcitrant synthetic dyes (e.g., anthraquinone and azo dyes), low-molecular-weight phenolics (e.g., guaiacol, catechol, hydroquinone, and 2,6-dimethoxyphenol), and lignin-derived aromatic compounds, supporting their role in lignin degradation processes.

sec.p: In the context of ligninolytic processes, lignin is a major byproduct of the Kraft pulping process that can be valorized into value-added products via enzymatic depolymerization through the cleavage of C–O and C–C bonds. Lignin oxidation can typically be analyzed by derivatization of carbonyl products with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine under acidic conditions. Biocatalysis thus offers a cost-effective and environmentally green tool for lignin valorization.

Beyond peroxidase activity, certain DyPs exhibit additional catalytic functionalities. Some enzymes display hydrolase-like activity; for example, the DyP from Bjerkandera adusta degrades reactive blue 5, with phthalic acid formation suggesting hydrolytic cleavage, potentially facilitated by water generated during the peroxidase cycle. Other typical class V DyPs, such as MscDyP from Marasmius scorodonius, demonstrate oxidase activity in the absence of H2O2, as evidenced by β-carotene oxidation, indicating bifunctional catalytic activity. Moreover, some DyP members (e.g., EfeB homologues) exhibit deferrochelatase-like activity, as the enzyme removes iron from heme without damaging the tetrapyrrole ring, unlike typical heme oxygenases.

The broad catalytic versatility of DyPs allows for their potential use in a range of biotechnological applications. In addition to dye decolorization and wastewater treatment, DyPs are also used for lignin depolymerization into value-added products.15 They also play a critical role in microbial cell physiology, including oxidation of metals such as Cu+ to Cu2+, developmental regulation, and cell protection from oxidative stress when enclosed within a bacterial nanocompartment (e.g., encapsulins). The ease of expression of DyPs, particularly with bacterial systems compared to fungal hosts, further highlights their potential for industrial and environmental applications, as well as emerging uses in biosensing and antimicrobial strategies.

DyPs exhibit various catalytic mechanisms depending on the nature of the substrate (size and structure). More specifically, two different oxidation sites are proposed in the enzyme: one at the heme pocket for low-molecular-weight, small substrates, and a second, distal surface site for larger substrates, which are sterically hindered from accessing the heme cavity.

Regarding the physicochemical properties of DyP peroxidases, the majority are heme-containing proteins with molecular weights around 50–60 kDa. , They exhibit high variability in oligomeric assemblies and can occur as monomers, dimers, tetramers, pentamers, or hexamers. DyP enzymes tend to retain high activity performance in acidic conditions. Despite this, some DyPs show higher catalytic performance at alkaline pH (7.0–8.0), such as SCDyP2 and SviDyP. On one hand, DyP enzymes typically show optimal activity at temperatures between 40 and 60 °C. On the other hand, other DyPs prefer different optimal temperatures, such as PpDyP and BsDyP, with optimal working temperatures between 10–30 °C and 20–30 °C, respectively. DyPs can be influenced by several metal ions that can either increase or decrease their activity. To use DyPs in industrial applications, it is important to optimize their tolerance to pH and temperature, by broadening the range in which they remain active.

This review reports the mutational effects on various DyP properties to explore significant variants that may increase their tolerance for broad utilization in different purposes. In this review, the role of each significant residue and the effect of mutational changes are discussed in a detailed manner to show these residues’ variation among the four DyP classes in function and mechanism of catalysis.

A set of rigorous eligibility criteria was developed to select the studies included in this review. First, only studies that examined DyPs across different biological domains (bacterial, fungal, and eukaryotic sources), with their main experimental analysis focused on the mutational effects on specific DyP properties and/or catalytic activity, were chosen. Studies that focused solely on non-DyP enzymes or examined only wild-type DyPs without experimentation on mutations were excluded. Second, primary research articles were selected, encompassing biochemical studies of DyPs, site-directed mutagenesis studies, and structural biology reports (e.g., X-ray crystallography). Third, review articles and book chapters were referenced only for context and historical perspective. Finally, the scope of mutagenesis studies’ was restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed articles published between 2007 and 2025.

Following application of the eligibility criteria, a total of 35 primary research articles were identified for qualitative synthesis. Collectively, these studies reported 93 different DyP mutations across 20 different DyPs derived from bacterial and fungal sources, with contributions of DyP types across the four phylogenetic groups as follows: class A (n = 8), class B (n = 6), class C (n = 1), and class D (n = 5). A systematic evaluation of the effects of mutations was conducted for these studies on the basis of the following major enzyme parameters: catalytic turnover, thermal and chemical stability, optimal working pH, and resistance to H2O2 inactivation. All of the studies reported an extensive range of functional results, from a positive enhancement to a negative perturbation of enzyme properties.

sec.title: Genetic Engineering Strategies Used for Altering DyP Properties
sec.p:
Several genetic engineering strategies can be applied to DyPs, such as site-directed mutagenesis, saturation mutagenesis, directed evolution, ,, and heterologous expression, −
to enhance their activity, stability, and suitability for industrial applications.

The most common protein engineering strategies are directed at conserved residues closely located near the heme center. For example, Li et al. employed rational design using myoglobin as a scaffold, implementing the incorporation of tyrosine/tryptophan (Y/W) residues and the presence of a conserved histidine-arginine (H-R) pair close to the heme active center via four mutations (F43Y/T67R/P88W/F138W). ,, As a result, artificial DyPs have been produced with catalytic efficiencies (k cat/K m) that are as much as 144 times higher than the wild-type myoglobin and even higher than some native DyPs. ,,

Each of the previously described mutagenesis strategies has contributed to improving DyP performance; however, their combined application is generally more effective. Integrating directed evolution with focused site-directed/saturation mutagenesis at identified hotspots results in multiparameter improvements. Among these approaches, directed evolution is often considered the most powerful standalone method due to its ability to produce large variant libraries with a wide range of desired properties, including enhanced catalytic activity, expanded substrate scope, improved pH tolerance, improved stability, greater H2O2 resistance, and higher expression yield. In contrast, rational approaches are particularly effective for targeted optimization.

sec.title: Saturation Mutagenesis
sec.p: Site-saturation mutagenesis targets specific amino acid positions and substitutes them with all possible residues, creating variant libraries with diverse physicochemical properties, often leading to moderate improvements in protein function. Site-saturation mutagenesis of conserved residues, including glutamate from flexible loops, produced DyP variants from Bacillus subtilis and Kitasatospora aureofaciens with greater catalytic performance toward 2,2′-azino-bis­(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS). The enhanced characteristics can be due to the electron transfer by the surface exposed tryptophans. Additionally, the genetically engineered glutamate may function as a pH-responsive switch to protect against intracellular oxidative stress.

sec.title: Directed Evolution
sec.p: Directed evolution is a lab technique that copies natural evolution but in a controlled setting. Directed evolution approaches, including error-prone PCR and saturation mutagenesis, have been successfully used to create DyP variants with improved catalytic activity and increased resistance to inactivation by H2O2. ,, After several rounds of mutagenesis, focused mutant libraries can be created and screened for enhanced oxidative activity along with other physicochemical properties. This process is repeated several times to gradually find the best version. ,,,

Directed evolution is scalable and can enhance DyP properties in industrial applications, including catalytic efficiency, substrate range, stability, pH tolerance, and expression yields, together resulting in low catalyst costs and adaptation to harsh industrial conditions. ,,, No major bottlenecks have been widely reported, and in some cases, evolved variants even show improved secretion and production. ,,,

For example, after three rounds of random mutagenesis by error-prone PCR (epPCR) and one round of saturation mutagenesis in DyP4 from Pleurotus ostreatus, the 4D4 variant (I56V, K109R, N227S, and N312S) was isolated. This variant showed desirable properties, including improved protein yield and secretion, 2.7 times higher catalytic efficiency, and 7-fold higher H2O2 tolerance (IC50). The four substitutions improved substrate accessibility, substrate binding affinity, and catalytic turnover at the active site. These properties increased and stabilized the enzyme activity under high levels of peroxide, which is required for industrial decolorization as well as for biotransformation of lignin.

Directed evolution was also utilized to enhance the catalytic efficiency of DyP1B from Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf-5 toward phenolic- and lignin-derived substrates (Table ). Focused mutant libraries were created from targeted saturation mutagenesis at seven residues in the heme-proximal active site region. These libraries were subsequently screened for enhanced oxidative activity using 2,6-dichlorophenol (DCP) as the model substrate. Targeted mutations to DyP1B significantly improved its catalytic activity, substrate profile, and stability to phenolic compounds, lignin derivatives, and Mn­(II).

sec.p: In DyP1B, the N193L and H169L variants showed a 7–8-fold increase in catalytic efficiency toward DCP, while the V205I/A209H variant increased catalytic activity toward alkali kraft lignin. H169 and F218 residues were shown to be important in facilitating a productive orientation and stabilization of the heme for catalysis. In addition, the F218R mutation provided an increase in thermostability due to the formation of additional hydrogen bonds between R218, the heme propionate, and the adjacent E216, suggesting potential for use in industrial biocatalysis.

Also, site-directed mutagenesis of S223, H127, and D154 residues was suggested to play a key role in the interaction between metals and substrates. , Mn2+ was observed to enhance the oxidation of polymeric lignin products. Therefore, rational design strategies targeted residues located at the Mn2+ binding site in order to improve lignin oxidation efficiency. , As a result, Mn2+ oxidation showed increased k cat /K m by 5-fold in the case of the H127R variant and 8-fold in the S223A variant. Furthermore, the S223A mutant increased the production of low-molecular-weight phenolic products from polymeric soda lignin by 2-fold. ,

Moreover, directed evolution was used to improve the catalytic efficiency of bacterial dye-decolorizing peroxidase PpDyP from Pseudomonas putida MET94 toward phenolic substrates. Several variants were produced with dramatically improved catalytic performance, broader substrate range, higher pH optima, and better resistance to inactivation by peroxide, all of which greatly increased the potential of PpDyP in lignin valorization and biorefinery applications. , After three consecutive rounds of random mutagenesis using error-prone PCR and high-throughput activity screening, three mutants were chosen for further investigation: 29E4 (E188K and H125Y), 6E10 (E188K, A142V, and H125Y), and 25F6 (E188K, A142V, H125Y, and G129D).

Among these mutants, 6E10 (E188K, A142V, and H125Y) displayed 100 times higher catalytic efficiency toward the substrate 2,6-dimethoxyphenol (DMP) in comparison to the wild-type enzyme, reaching the efficiency of fungal lignin peroxidases. The 6E10 variant also showed higher activity toward syringyl and guaiacyl-type phenolics, aromatic amines, Kraft lignin (2.5-fold higher than wild-type activity), and the lignin model dimer guaiacylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (70% conversion yield after 1 h vs 20% conversion yield in wild type). , In addition, the 6E10 variant resulted in a notable alkaline shift in optimal pH from 4.5 (wild type) to 8.5, as well as a higher tolerance to H2O2 than the original enzyme and 2-fold higher production yield, improving the possibilities for catalysis under conditions that are relevant to industrial bioprocessing. ,

The substitution A142V, found in 6E10, affects a small α-helix E140-A146, adjacent to the loop D117-D139, containing the catalytic distal heme residues. A142V stabilized the loop into a more flexible state, allowing substrates to diffuse to the heme pocket and improve turnover, at the cost of structural stabilization. , The substitution altered the electrostatic environment of the heme pocket, changing the pK a of catalytic residues, shifting the optimum pH toward neutral and alkaline values and protecting the sensitive amino acids near the heme cavity against H2O2 oxidative effects. , The substitutions H125Y (located near the distal heme region) and E188K (located in a surface loop at the entrance of the heme access channel) also altered electrostatics and hydrogen-bonding networks surrounding the heme, leading to modification of the enzyme reactivity. , In the case of E188K, the positively charged lysine residue favored the accommodation of the anionic ABTS substrate, resulting in its oxidation. , These observations emphasize the effectiveness of combining loop-focused engineering with directed evolution to optimize DyP properties.

In the case of immobilized enzyme, 29E4 and wild-type PpDyP retained high stability and activity, while 6E10 and 25F6 were less effective and inhibited at higher levels of H2O2, suggesting that A142V and G129D had improved catalysis during soluble-phase use, while lowered robustness during immobilized and oxidative stress events.

Overall, directed evolution generally yields broad, substantial improvements, particularly for complex substrates such as lignin. Rational design is valuable for mechanistic insight and targeted modifications but is most effective when combined with evolutionary approaches. ,,

sec.title: Heterologous Expression
sec.p: DyP genes have been heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli and Trichoderma atroviride for load-scale production and streamlined screening of engineered variants. Generally, E. coli is considered the preferred host for DyP peroxidase expression due to its rapid growth, low cost, and high protein yield. However, limitations such as improper folding and reduced enzymatic activity may occur, requiring optimization strategies to improve protein recovery. Consequently, alternative hosts, particularly filamentous fungi, are increasingly explored, owing to their ability to mediate eukaryotic post-translational modifications and aid efficient protein secretion.

When coexpressed with secretion-enhancing proteins (such as OsmY), it was easier to achieve extracellular secretion and conduct high-throughput activity experiments than before the coexpression process. , In fact, recombinant DyPs expressed in these systems have shown efficient dye decolorization as well as improved biocatalytic performance in whole-cell approaches. ,

Another example of heterologous expression in DyPs is DyP2, a type C DyP that lacks an N-terminal signal sequence necessary for being secreted outside of the cell. To allow for secretion in S. lividans TK24, the heterologous signal peptide from Bacillus subtilis DyP (BsDyP) was successfully cloned into the pIJ plasmid upstream and in-frame to the DyP2 coding sequence (the DyP2 sequence came from Amycolatopsis 75iv2).

sec.title: Structure–Function Insights from Mutational Studies of DyP-Type Peroxidases
sec.p: Examples of engineered DyP-type peroxidases were compiled to examine how site-directed mutations at distinct structural and functional regions influence enzyme properties (Table ). The collected studies encompass substitutions targeting key catalytic residues, including the distal arginine, proximal histidine, and conserved GXXDG motif, in addition to mutations introduced outside the canonical active site (Figure ).

caption.p: Comparative Sequence Analysis of DyPs. A multiple sequence alignment was performed by MEGA version 12, with subsequent visualization using Jalview version 2.11.4.1. The figure shows the mutation sites across DyPs from the four classes (A, B, C, and D) and the recurrent mutational hotspots. Significant hotspots are labeled numerically and boxed in red-colored groups. The targeted amino acids undergoing mutational changes are highlighted in magenta color. The highly conserved residues (with conservation score 8+) are boxed in green-colored groups.

sec.p: Additional variants involve residues located in long-range electron transfer (LRET) pathways and in conserved loops and substrate access tunnels that guide substrates toward the heme center. By analyzing these studies, we aimed to identify structural hotspots that govern the function and robustness of DyP-type peroxidases. Hence, a framework for the rational engineering of DyP enzymes with improved properties for industrial and biotechnological applications can be applied.

Structure–function predictions for regions outside the canonical active site in DyPs derived from structure-based studies (e.g., X-ray crystallography) and computational approaches (e.g., molecular dynamics (MD) simulations), are generally qualitatively reliable. Numerous engineering studies on DyPs have shown that these approaches can successfully point out key regions and candidate residues responsible for substrate access and electron transfer. However, such predictions are not sufficient on their own and must be backed up by detailed experimental validation. Quantitative analyses, including mutagenesis, kinetic analysis, and stability measurements, are necessary to confirm and refine these predictions.

In the PpDyP 6E10 variant, structural analysis and MD simulations precisely linked increased loop flexibility and changes in tunnel shape to the experimentally observed enhancement in catalytic efficiency, albeit with reduced stability. In addition, constant-pH MD simulations correctly predicted changes in the heme electrostatic environment that were consistent with the observed alkaline pH shift. Similarly, in KpDyP, computational MD simulations and structural analyses identified surface-exposed radical residues and electron-transfer pathways, which were subsequently validated by EPR (electron paramagnetic resonance) and mutagenesis studies.

In AauDyP, combined PELE (Protein Energy Landscape Exploration) simulations and QM/MM (quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics) calculations revealed a high-turnover radical site (W77) alongside a secondary low-turnover site located at the heme access channel. Both sites were involved in electron transfer from bulky substrates through the LRET pathway. These predictions were later corroborated by mutagenesis and EPR analyses, supporting their qualitative reliability. Collectively, these findings emphasize that predictive approaches provide important qualitative insights which, when integrated with experimental data, enable highly reliable structure–function characterization.

sec.title: Mutations Introduced within the Active Site Region of DyP-Type Peroxidases
sec.p: The conserved active-site triad (H–R–D) in DyPs is part of the coordination of heme iron, substrate binding, and ultimately enzyme catalysis. Site-directed mutagenesis of the proximal and distal heme domain residues has been conducted in DyP classes to determine the structural and functional properties upon changing these residues. Although the active-site triad (H–R–D) appears to be conserved within DyPs, the effect of any of these mutations was shown to be dependent on DyP class, substrate type, and structural context.

sec.title: Proximal Histidine Mutational Effects on DyP Activity and Properties
sec.p: Similar to the proximal histidine ligand in plant peroxidases (e.g., H170 in HRP), the histidine residue in DyPs is a noncovalently coordinated axial (fifth) heme iron ligand. , The central heme iron is coordinated by a histidine on the proximal side, and this histidine, along with the hydrogen-bonding interactions, forms an essential basis for heme stability and active-site integrity. The proximal histidine is designated as Site 1 (Figure ), which confirms proximal histidine conservation among all DyP classes, highlighting its significant role in the DyP catalytic cycle. Its substitution by a noncoordinating residue via mutagenesis invariably resulted in a complete loss of activity across the spectrum of tested substrates (Table ). This loss of activity can be attributed to the inability to recreate the enzyme’s resting state, as evidenced by TcDyP.

sec.title: Distal Aspartate Mutational Effects on DyPs Activity and Properties
sec.p: The distal heme side of DyPs is where catalysis occurs at the interface of the substrate channels. On the heme distal side, the H2O2-binding pocket is created by four conserved residues: a catalytic aspartate, a catalytic arginine, and two hydrophobic residues. ,, The specific roles of the distal aspartate and arginine residues in DyPs are poorly understood. Research has suggested that aspartate serves as a functional replacement for the distal histidine characteristic of plant peroxidases.

Moreover, aspartate shows high variability. It is replaced by alanine or serine in subclass I1, glutamate in subclasses I3 and P2, and is less conserved in subclass I2. While glutamate can serve to replace the catalytic base in compound I formation, aspartate is generally more efficient. Despite acidic character preservation, the bulky glutamate residue may result in inhibition of substrate access to the heme and activity reduction. As proof, the E → D mutation in CboDyP resulted in a 10-fold increase in catalytic activity toward reactive blue 19 (RB19) at pH 4, mainly due to the smaller size of aspartate (Figure ). Moreover, replacing the conserved aspartate with glutamate in TfuDyP and SviDyP diminished their activity by 2–5-fold compared to their wild types, confirming aspartate as the optimal residue in that position. , Still, the considerable residual activity in all tested DyPs with the D to E substitution suggests that the DyP signature sequence motif could be better described as GXX­[D/E]­G.

caption.p: CboDyP E201D variant crystal structure showing the bulky E201 residue (magenta-colored) and an overlay substitution with a smaller aspartate residue (white-colored).

sec.p: In mutagenesis studies, where the aspartate residue (designated as site 2) was substituted, a significant decrease or complete loss of peroxidase activity toward different tested substrates (including catechol, ABTS, RB19, RB5, and phenol) was observed. ,, These reports are consistent with the fact that the distal aspartate residue acts as a proton acceptor essential for H2O2 binding, activation, and deprotonation. Hence, compound I formation represents the rate-limiting step in the peroxidation of the mentioned substrates. It is worth mentioning that there is an exception: the guaiacol substrate in class A DyPs relies on compound II formation as the rate-limiting step in the peroxidation reaction. , However, YfeX from class B showed a decreased catalytic efficiency toward guaiacol upon replacing the distal aspartate, which confirms the role of this residue in the oxidation of phenolic substrates in class B DyPs.

The distal aspartate was replaced in class A, B, and D DyPs with asparagine, alanine, histidine, or valine (Table ). On one hand, replacing the acidic aspartate residue with the neutral asparagine, alanine, valine, or basic histidine may inhibit the main residue function as a proton acceptor, subsequently compound I formation. On the other hand, the same D→N substitution resulted in an increased catalytic efficiency toward ABTS, acid blue 62, and mordant black 9 in BsDyP and ABTS in PpDyP. ,, This enhanced catalytic activity supports the distal aspartate’s essential role in optimal H2O2 binding to the heme group, but not strictly individually necessary for H2O2 (de)­protonation or O–O bond cleavage. Also, the distal aspartate substitution in certain DyPs does not disrupt the enzyme hydrogen-bonding network or tunnel architecture.

sec.title: Distal Arginine Mutational Effects on DyP Activity and Properties
sec.p: The conserved distal arginine (designated as site 3) has a stabilizing interaction with the heme propionate via a hydrogen bond network and is essential for heme incorporation, heme propionate stabilization, compound I formation, and stabilization of the architecture of the substrate access tunnels. The catalytic significance of the distal arginine is confirmed by the high level of preservation (nearly 100%) of this residue in all DyP classes (Figure ). It has been shown that mutational changes in this residue eliminate enzyme activity and Soret band appearance (Table ). ,,,

It is observed that, from the 11 distal arginine variants mentioned in Table , only one variant enhanced the catalytic activity of the enzyme (BsDyP, similar to its distal aspartate variant). This observation confirms the indispensable role of the distal arginine residue in different DyP classes, especially toward the anthraquinone substrates. It is proposed that the substitution of arginine with leucine, alanine, glutamine, or glutamate abolishes the basic character and the positively charged guanidinium group. These properties are essential for important electrostatic interactions that orient H2O2 in a productive manner for binding and heterolytic cleavage. Thus, the distal arginine mutations contribute to poor compound I formation and a diminished ability to discriminate between reactive oxygen species (ROS).

The distal arginine role is also observed to be substrate-dependent. For example, YfeX DyP requires arginine in RB19 and ABTS oxidation, while phenolic substrates such as guaiacol and catechol are less dependent. Some studies have previously suggested that this residue plays a lesser role in A- and D-type DyPs when compared with B-type DyPs. , However, recent work has shown that the distal arginine is also mechanistically required for A- and D-type DyPs, and this is assumed to have a functionally relevant potential role for all DyP-family enzymes.

sec.title: Distal Asparagine Mutational Effects on DyP Activity and Properties
sec.p: Distal asparagine (designated as Site 4) was observed to affect acid–base catalysis, but to a very small extent. The distal asparagine mutants showed relatively little impact on the enzyme catalytic potential (as shown in PpDyP , ), which confirms that the distal asparagine does not participate in the peroxidation reaction in a direct way. Regarding the electrostatic environment, the pK a values in the active site and the optimal working pH of the enzymes were affected upon N→L substitution. Therefore, the distal asparagine residue was assumed to play an important role in optimizing the pH for the oxidation reaction in the DyP family. Moreover, the N→L substitution led to a higher catalytic potential in BsDyP (4–50-fold across various substrates) and PpDyP (2-fold with ABTS) , suggesting the better accommodation of leucine at this position than in the original enzyme and that this residue plays an important role in catalysis in BsDyP and PpDyP.

sec.title: Mutations Introduced into the Fifth Glycine Residue in the GXXDG Motif of DyPs
sec.p: The conserved DyP fingerprint motif, GXXDG, exhibits an unusual substitution at the fifth position in the DrDyP (class C), where methionine (M190) serves as a surrogate for the canonical glycine found in other DyPs. The functional significance of this unusual residue was therefore investigated. UV–Vis and resonance Raman spectroscopy revealed that the DrDyP M190G variant remained in a six-coordinate low-spin (6cLS) state at pH 7.5, demonstrating that the methionine substitution does not affect enzyme activity.

sec.title: Mutations Introduced into the Conserved Loops and Tunnel Regions of DyP-Type Peroxidases
sec.p: DyPs exhibit conserved flexible loop domains that partially cover their heme-containing reactive site. These loops are expected to play a regulatory role with respect to substrate accessibility, electron transfer pathways, and catalytic utilization. For this reason, many mutagenesis studies have targeted residues within these loops and tunnels to probe effects on the physicochemical properties of the enzyme. ,,

Substitutions in these regions are predicted to affect the catalytic cycle via multiple mechanisms. Modifications (or mutations) to these regions by introducing bulky side chains impacted enzymatic activity by blocking the loops and tunnels and obstructing the access of substrate or cofactor to the catalytic site, as seen in EfeB/YcdB Q68W and YfeX S234Y variants. In contrast, substitution with smaller residues increased tunnel width and loop flexibility, enhancing substrate diffusion and turnover; however, often at the cost of structural stability, as seen in the TfuDyP F336A variant (Figure ). Interestingly, substitution of the bulky phenylalanine in TfuDyP with the smaller alanine residue exhibits substrate-dependent features, where this substitution greatly enhances ABTS oxidation without affecting phenol oxidation. This behavior can be attributed to the larger size of ABTS, which benefits from increased loop flexibility or widening of the substrate access channel, in contrast to the smaller phenolic substrates that are less dependent on such structural changes.

sec.p: Moreover, certain residues (such as E309Q and E309L in KaDyP1, E312W and E312F in BsDyP) may act as pH-dependent switches, modulating the architecture of the distal heme cavity and influencing electron transfer pathways. Other modifications altered residues characteristics such as loop flexibility, electron tunneling pathways, reorganization of the distal heme cavity, electrostatics, and hydrogen-bonding networks that play essential roles in enzyme catalysis, as observed in D242A and H338A in TfuDyP and E188K, A142V, H125Y, and G129D in PpDyP. ,

Strategic engineering of loop or tunnel residues can be used to modify the electron access pathways and change the selectivity and kinetics of the enzyme (taking into consideration the size and chemical properties of the introduced residues).

sec.title: Mutations Introduced at Surface-Exposed Residues Constituting the LRET Pathway in DyP-Type Peroxidases
sec.p: Like anthraquinone dyes, large substrates are oxidized by exposed radical sites on the enzyme surface, most often tryptophan or tyrosine residues. These residues act as radical relay sites by transferring electrons to the heme from the substrate-binding sites. Specific mutations in DyPs can be engineered into the LRET pathway to enhance oxidation of bulky substrates. These mutations are generally made at surface-exposed residues that are thought to shepherd electron flow and substrate access. The mutational targets include various primary and secondary radical sites observed in different DyP classes (sites 5–20 in Figure ). Secondary radical sites potentially cooperate with primary radical sites (Table ), but they are less essential for catalytic activity. ,

sec.p: Both primary and secondary sites are shown to be substrate-specific. For example, substitution of site 6 tyrosine (Y374 in DtpA and Y337 in AauDyP1) reduced the catalytic efficiency toward ABTS without any effect on RB19 oxidation. , Also, site 8 tryptophan and sites 9 and 10 tyrosine (W18, Y92, and Y247 in KpDyP) and site 18 tryptophan (W377 in AauDyP1) were shown to be essential for ABTS oxidation. The following residues were observed to have an essential role in RB19 oxidation reaction: site 5 and 7 tryptophan (W263 and W376 in TcDyP), , sites 6 and 13 tyrosine (Y235 and Y129 in VcDyP), , at low pH, site 16 histidine (H178 in VcDyP), , and site 18 tryptophan (W377 in AauDyP1). These studies allow for the prediction of essential radical sites for various substrates in the corresponding DyPs (Figure ).

In addition to primary and secondary radical sites, other sites were found to be essential in the LRET pathway for the stabilization of tyrosyl and tryptophanyl radical sites by hydrogen bond networks, , as shown in the W263–W376 dyad in TcDyP and Y247–Y92 and Y247–W18 dyads in KpDyP (W18 corresponds to site 8 and Y92 corresponds to site 9 in Figure ). In addition, they can assist the electron-transfer pathway between the heme and substrates. , Therefore, these auxiliary radical sites should be considered when engineering DyP members, as their mutations may lead to the loss of radical formation and catalytic activity.

sec.title: Mutational Impacts on the Optimal Working pH and Stability of DyP-Type Peroxidases
sec.p: DyP enzymes tend to retain high activity performance in acidic conditions. This fact may limit DyPs’ biotechnological and industrial applications. Therefore, mutagenesis studies aimed at increasing the optimal working pH of certain DyP members toward the neutral to alkaline range.

In VcDyP, D138 (site 15) was observed to be the determinant of optimal working pH in the case of guaiacol as a substrate, while in PpDyP, the distal D132N variant produced higher optimal pH (7.4) compared to the wild-type enzyme (pHopt = 4.3) using ABTS as a substrate. Therefore, certain aspartate residues may have a role in the retention of high activity of DyPs in acidic conditions. Substitution of these residues with neutral or alkaline ones may optimize the enzymatic activity toward neutral to alkaline conditions. This fact may be valid in the case of D132N in PpDyP , and D138V in VcDyP; however, in other cases, similar mutations may not affect the optimal working pH of enzymes (as in D144H in VcDyP , ). Moreover, the distal asparagine residue was observed to play an important role in optimizing the pH for the oxidation reaction in the DyP family, as evidenced by the N136L variant in PpDyP. ,

In addition, the optimal pH was lowered to 3.6 in the case of the PpDyP R214L mutant, supporting a cooperative interaction between D132 and R214 in the acid–base mechanism. This effect can be explained by shifting pH optima to values closer to the pKa value of arginine (12.48) in the absence of aspartate in the D132N variant and the opposite shift of pH optima to values closer to the pKa value of aspartate (3.9) in the R214L variant.

Enzyme stability can be affected by mutations introduced into the conserved loops (Table ). Loop versatility is considered to be a major contributor to activity and stability. These mutations may alter the electrostatics and hydrogen-bonding networks that surround the heme, modifying the stability and reactivity of the enzyme (as shown in Table , E312 variants in BsDyP and E309 variants in KaDyP1).

sec.title: Substrate-Specific Effects of Catalytic Residues
sec.p: Catalytic mechanism and the role of conserved residues differ within the four DyP classes and with different substrates/substrate types within the same class. Studies on various DyPs were reviewed, and residues’ roles in the catalytic cycle of various substrates were analyzed, including H2O2, phenolic substrates (such as catechol and guaiacol), anthraquinone dyes (such as ABTS, RB19, acid blue 62, and mordant black 9), Mn2+, hydroquinone, DCP, DMP, and lignin derivatives.

The functional impact of conserved catalytic residues in DyPs is highly substrate- and class-dependent, as these residues operate within interconnected catalytic networks involving the heme pocket, substrate access tunnels, radical transfer pathways, and local electrostatics. Their roles can vary depending on the substrate size, redox potential, and binding mode, which in turn influence the rate-limiting step and interaction patterns. Consequently, modification of a single residue may differentially affect the oxidation of distinct substrates. Furthermore, these effects can vary across DyP classes, where differences in the surrounding structural architecture modulate the functional contributions of conserved residues.

In the catalytic activity of H2O2, mutations introduced into the distal aspartate and arginine residues confirmed the indispensable roles of these residues in modulating H2O2 binding, stabilization, deprotonation, and O–O bond cleavage inside the heme active site in all DyP classes. Except for BsDyP, the importance of those distal heme residues in H2O2 catalysis was not fully confirmed. Other mutational studies confirmed the essential role of loop and tunnel residues in enhancing H2O2 access and arrival at the heme active site, as shown in YfeX and DyP4. ,

Phenolic substrates have a small size, which proves the great effect of loop- and tunnel-forming residues and their mutations on these substrates’ access to the active site. Also, mutational studies confirmed the essential role of the distal aspartate and proximal histidine residues in DyP classes (A, B, and D), while the distal arginine residue was shown to be less significant for this group of substrates (Table ). Exceptionally, the distal arginine greatly affected the catalytic potential of TfuDyP toward phenol.

Studies on anthraquinone substrates (including ABTS, RB19, acid blue 62, and mordant black 9) showed that various DyP classes (A, B, and D) depend on the distal aspartate as a proton acceptor for compound I formation. It was found that the catalytic efficiency of DyPs decreased in the absence of this distal residue (Table ). However, in the case of BsDyP, the roles of both distal aspartates and arginines have not yet been fully elucidated.

The conserved proximal histidine residue was observed to have a significant role in enzyme stabilization and heme coordination with anthraquinone substrates. In addition, the distal arginine was found to have an indispensable role in anthraquinones’ oxidation in classes A, B, and D. This fact was proved by the total loss of catalytic activity toward anthraquinones in the case of distal arginine mutants compared with partial loss of activity in the case of distal aspartate mutants (Table ).

Being bulky in size, anthraquinones cannot enter the active heme site and depend mainly on the surface characteristics of DyPs via the LRET pathway to be oxidized. Therefore, mutations introduced into the surface radical residues greatly affected anthraquinones’ oxidation, in addition to other loop residues that facilitate electron transfer along the LRET pathway (Table ). Distinct surface-exposed radical sites are used for substrate oxidation in a substrate-dependent manner. For example, ABTS oxidation involved Y374 in DtpA, Y247 and Y92 in KpDyP, and Y337 and W377 in AauDyP, while RB19 utilized alternative tyrosine residues (Y109, Y133, Y129, and Y235) and H178 in VcDyP , according to the working pH conditions.

sec.title: Future Perspectives
sec.p: Future research on DyPs should follow six coordinated paths. First, a systematic investigation of catalytically important regions, along with cutting-edge protein engineering in newly discovered DyPs, can greatly improve biotechnological and environmental applications of DyPs, including wastewater treatment and lignin valorization.

A second path would involve systematic analysis of conserved but not functionally characterized regions such as S20–S27, S29, S30, and S31 (Figure ), which would likely discover new structural motifs or residues with regulatory or catalytic roles. Those residues might be conserved in a particular DyP class or among all DyP classes (A–D). This would deepen the understanding of enzyme mechanism and facilitate rational enzyme design.

The development of enhanced computational techniques to assess the effects of a particular mutation on catalytic activity, as well as physicochemical properties in DyPs, is another approach. This approach can predict which residues located at the enzyme’s active sites or on the enzyme surface(s) are involved in binding distinct substrates or substrate classes. Computational analyses can further elucidate the local substrate environment and aid in the rational prediction of beneficial substitutions that optimize enzyme activity and selectivity with the least investment in both time and resources before conducting practical experimental studies.

A fourth priority is the systematic study of residues that modulate hydrogen-bonding networks and electrostatic interactions within DyPs. Understanding these contributions is essential for widening the operational pH range of DyPs and improving their thermal and chemical stabilities under harsh conditions relevant to biotechnological and industrial applications.

A fifth approach focuses on the long-range electron-transfer (LRET) pathway and the specific role of surface-exposed radical sites in the oxidation of bulky substrates. In particular, the mechanism by which electrons are transferred from the buried heme to the enzyme surface, as well as strategies to control these pathways, remains incompletely understood. As noted by Yoshida and Sugano, this ambiguity largely arises from the lack of crystallized structural evidence for genuine enzyme–substrate (ES) complexes with bulky aromatic substrates in DyPs. To date, the only reported ES complex involves binding of 2,6-dimethoxyphenol near N313 in class V DyP from B. adusta, linked via a hydrogen-bonding network to the heme propionate. In contrast, binding sites for bulkier molecules, such as synthetic dyes, remain unidentified.

Finally, further studies are required to understand the exact roles of distal heme ligands, including the conserved distal aspartate, arginine, and asparagine. Elucidating how these residues participate in substrate oxidation across different DyP members and reaction conditions will provide more insight regarding their essentiality in the catalytic mechanism.
